conceptTag: Pick a beachhead for a new tool
readerTitle: Twenty trades liked her app. Which one should she win first?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (주택 서비스용 견적·일정 앱, 냉장 운송용 온도 센서) · 수치 없음
insight: 새 도구의 첫 시장은 가장 큰 곳이 아니라, 같은 고통을 겪고 서로 추천하며 다음 시장으로 이어지는 좁은 곳이다.
misconception: 관심을 보이는 고객이 많을수록 좋으니 처음부터 넓게 팔아야 한다.

sources.text: Moore, G. A. (1991). Crossing the Chasm. HarperBusiness. (교두보 시장, 볼링핀 전략 개념)

factChecks.note: 모든 사례는 가상입니다. 실제 통계나 기업 사실은 쓰지 않았습니다. Moore의 교두보·볼링핀 개념 설명이 원전과 맞는지 게시 전에 확인하세요.

cards.title: Twenty trades liked her app. None of them spread it.
body: Maya built a simple app that lets home service pros send quotes and plan their day from a phone.
Plumbers, painters, cleaners, electricians and pool techs all tried it and said it was nice. A few kept using it. Nobody told a friend. Six months in, she has scattered users and no momentum.

image.label: A phone app surrounded by many different tradespeople
image.brief: 휴대폰 화면 하나를 중심으로 배관공, 페인터, 청소부, 전기공, 수영장 관리사 등 여러 직업 인물이 흩어져 서로 등을 돌리고 있는 모습. 3D 클레이 스타일, 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Where should Maya focus first?
body: She has money and time for one focused push. Which group should she try to win?

options.text: All home service pros in her city, with ads aimed at everyone
options.feedback: Wide reach, but each trade has different needs and doesn't talk to the others. Her effort spreads thin and no group gets a full solution.

options.text: Pool service companies in her metro area
options.feedback: This is a **beachhead market**: a narrow group with the same weekly-route pain who meet at the same supply stores. She can win most of them and let word travel.

options.text: Electricians, because they spend the most on jobs
options.feedback: Big spending is attractive, but her app doesn't solve an urgent electrician problem yet. Size matters less than a shared, painful need she can own.

cards.title: Why pool techs make a good beachhead.
body: A beachhead is the first market you aim to dominate, so you can use it to reach the next one. Pool companies pass the tests:
list: **Shared pain:** the same houses every week, and chemical logs kept on paper
**Reason to buy now:** missed visits mean lost customers
**They talk:** same suppliers, same local groups
**Small enough to win:** a few hundred companies, not a few hundred thousand
cards.callout: Winning most of a small market beats a little of a big one.

cards.title: The first users were not the real test.
body: Maya's early users were tinkerers who liked trying new apps. The mainstream pool owner is different. Geoffrey Moore called the gap between those groups **the chasm**.

Practical buyers want two things: proof from someone just like them, and a tool that does the whole job. So Maya adds route planning and chemical logs, and asks happy owners to speak at the supply store.

image.label: A gap between early adopters and mainstream buyers, bridged by a pool-tech reference
image.brief: 왼쪽 절벽에 소수의 얼리어답터, 오른쪽 절벽에 다수의 일반 고객. 그 사이 틈을 '같은 업종 추천'과 '완성된 기능'이라는 두 판자가 잇는 다리. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: She has won 40 pool companies. What now?
body: Growth in pool service is slowing. Where should she go next?

options.text: Open the app to every trade nationwide
options.feedback: Fast on paper, but it repeats the original scatter. Each new trade lacks peers who can vouch for the tool.

options.text: Target lawn and irrigation companies, who run similar weekly routes
options.feedback: An adjacent segment that reuses most of the product and can trust pool-tech references. Like bowling pins, one win knocks over the next.

options.text: Keep adding pool features until every competitor is beaten
options.feedback: It deepens the beachhead, but a beachhead is meant to be a starting point, not the whole business.

cards.title: Narrow is not the same as dead-end.
body: A beachhead can be too small to pay the bills, or so unusual that nothing nearby needs the same tool. Then winning it leads nowhere.
Before committing, sketch the next two segments it could open. And set a time limit: if the group isn't buying after a fair try, pick another one rather than widening.

cards.title: Now it's a pallet temperature sensor.
body: A small manufacturer makes a clip-on sensor that records the temperature of a pallet during transport. Which first market fits best?

options.text: National grocery chains, for the biggest volume
options.feedback: Huge orders, but these are cautious buyers who want peer references the company doesn't have yet. It could stall in long trials.

options.text: Seafood distributors in one port region who argue over spoiled loads
options.feedback: A painful, shared problem, buyers who know each other, and a clear path to other chilled-food shippers. A classic beachhead.

options.text: Anyone who asks for a demo on the website
options.feedback: Easy early sales from enthusiasts, but they're scattered across industries and won't build the references mainstream buyers need.

cards.softwareNote: The same logic applies to the sensor's tracking dashboard: build reports seafood buyers need first, not settings for every possible customer.

cards.title: Win one tight group, then use it to reach the next.
body: You used two ideas: the **beachhead market** (pick a narrow group you can dominate) and **crossing the chasm** (mainstream buyers want peer proof and a complete tool).
**Try it today:** list three groups that could buy your new product. For each, write the shared pain and where its members talk to each other.
